team_text:
Registration request for a new AI use case. The system is called VoicePulse. The Head of Contact Centre Operations owns it. It is a vendor product that we license as SaaS. The vendor is a Dubai-based analytics firm and the product is VoicePulse Analytics. It analyses the voice tone of our call-centre agents during customer calls to infer stress, frustration and fatigue levels, and gives each agent a daily wellbeing score. Team leaders use the agents' wellbeing scores in coaching sessions and the scores are included in the quarterly performance review of each agent. It is used for managing call-centre staff, so it is an HR and workforce management use. It must not be used for disciplinary action on its own. Team leaders and the contact centre manager see the dashboard; they had a one-hour vendor training. About 180 call-centre agents are affected because their voices are analysed and scored. Yes, every score is about an individual agent. About 180 agents and roughly 40,000 calls per month. Some agents are young first-job employees; nothing specific is done for them. No, all agents are in Pakistan. It only produces scores; team leaders decide what to do. Team leaders review the scores weekly and can ignore them, but they usually discuss low scores with the agent. Call audio recordings of agents, call metadata and agent IDs. It processes voice recordings, which are biometric data of the agents. It uses voice features to recognise emotions, so it is emotion recognition. Audio is streamed to the vendor's cloud in the UAE. It is a deep neural network audio model provided by the vendor. No, it does not generate content; it outputs scores. No, agents do not interact with it; it runs in the background on calls. It reads call recordings from the telephony platform and writes scores to the vendor dashboard. It shows which call segments drove the score, but not why. Agents were told in a team meeting that calls are analysed for quality.

team_text:
Registering a staff wellbeing tool for the contact centre. VoicePulse is a vendor SaaS product that helps team leaders support agents who may be having a hard day, by highlighting calls where an agent sounded under pressure. Team leaders use it to start supportive coaching conversations. It runs in the background on call recordings and does not generate any content. The Head of Contact Centre Operations owns it and it is in a three-month pilot.

team_text:
We would like to register an AI use case. It is called TrustLens. The Head of Digital Onboarding owns it. It is a vendor product. The vendor is a regional fintech data company and the product is TrustLens Social. It is in development and planned for launch next quarter. It gives every new and existing digital customer a trust score built from their public social media activity, online behaviour and the trust scores of their contacts. Customers with a low trust score are automatically restricted to basic accounts, denied debit card upgrades and charged higher transfer fees. It is used in customer onboarding and account management. It should not be used for credit decisions. The digital onboarding team configures the score bands. All digital customers and applicants are affected, including people who only appear as contacts of customers. Yes, the score is calculated for each individual. Around 60,000 customers and applicants a month. Young people and low-income users with little online presence may score lower; nothing is done about it yet. We have no EU customers and no output is used in the EU. Restrictions are applied automatically without human review. There is no human review before restrictions apply; the team reviews score bands quarterly. Public social media posts, follower networks, app usage behaviour and contact lists. It processes customer personal data from social media and the app. No biometric data is used. The vendor trained it on data from its other clients; we have not seen it. The vendor processes data in its Singapore cloud. A vendor machine learning model using graph features. No, it produces a score only. No, customers do not interact with it. It reads from the onboarding platform and writes restriction flags to the core banking system. The vendor claims the score predicts account misuse with an AUC of 0.71. The score is a black box; no reasons are produced. Inputs and outputs are logged and kept for two years. Customers are not told about the score.

team_text:
Registration request for a new AI use case. We call it FaceSegment. The Head of Marketing owns it. Our data science team built it in-house. It is a prototype. It analyses the onboarding selfie of each customer to infer their likely religious sect, level of religiosity and ethnicity, so that marketing can segment customers for product campaigns. The inferred segment decides which product campaigns and offers each customer receives in the app. It is a marketing segmentation use. It will not be used for credit. The marketing analytics team uses the segments. Every customer who completes digital onboarding with a selfie is affected. Yes, each customer gets an inferred segment. About 25,000 new customers a month. No output is used in the EU and no affected people are in the EU. Segments are assigned automatically and campaigns are sent automatically. Onboarding selfie images and declared demographic data. It processes facial images, which are biometric data. We labelled 8,000 historical selfies using staff judgement. It does not generate any text, image or other content. No, customers do not interact with it. Reads selfies from the onboarding image store and writes segments to the marketing platform. It agrees with staff labels 74% of the time. Not tested. Inputs and outputs are logged and kept for two years.

obligations.title: AI literacy
obligations.text: Providers and deployers take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf.

obligations.title: Risk management system
obligations.text: A continuous, iterative risk management process across the lifecycle: identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights; estimate risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluate post-market data; adopt targeted risk management measures; test the system; give specific consideration to persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

obligations.title: Data and data governance
obligations.text: Training, validation and testing data subject to governance practices covering design choices, data collection processes and origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability and suitability, examination for possible biases likely to affect health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases, and identification of data gaps. Data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and as free of errors and complete as possible. Art. 10(5) allows processing special categories of personal data strictly for bias detection and correction, with safeguards.

obligations.title: Technical documentation
obligations.text: Technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date: general description, intended purpose, development process, design specifications, data requirements, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures and metrics, risk management system, changes over the lifecycle, standards applied, post-market monitoring plan.

obligations.title: Record-keeping
obligations.text: Technical capability for automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, enabling identification of risk situations, post-market monitoring and monitoring of operation.

obligations.title: Transparency and information to deployers
obligations.text: Designed so deployers can interpret output and use it appropriately; accompanied by instructions for use with the provider's identity, characteristics, capabilities and limitations, intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances leading to risks, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data specifications, human oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance, and log collection mechanisms.

obligations.title: Human oversight
obligations.text: Designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons during use. Oversight measures enable the assigned persons to: understand capacities and limitations and monitor operation; remain aware of automation bias; correctly interpret output; decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output; intervene or interrupt through a stop button or similar procedure.

obligations.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligations.text: Appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout the lifecycle. Accuracy levels and metrics declared in instructions for use. Resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies; feedback loops addressed; resilient against attempts to alter use or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities (data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks).

obligations.title: Provider obligations and quality management system
obligations.text: Providers ensure compliance with Section 2, have a quality management system, keep documentation and logs, undergo conformity assessment (Art. 43), draw up an EU declaration of conformity (Art. 47), affix CE marking (Art. 48), register (Art. 49), take corrective actions (Art. 20) and demonstrate conformity on request.

obligations.title: Responsibilities along the value chain
obligations.text: A deployer or other third party becomes a provider of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on it, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk.

obligations.title: Deployer obligations
obligations.text: Deployers: use the system according to instructions (26(1)); assign human oversight to persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (26(2)); ensure input data under their control is relevant and sufficiently representative (26(4)); monitor operation and inform the provider, and suspend use if it presents a risk; report serious incidents (26(5)); keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (26(6)); inform workers' representatives before use in the workplace (26(7)); inform natural persons that they are subject to a high-risk system that makes or assists decisions about them (26(11)).

obligations.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
obligations.text: Before deployment, bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III 5(b) (creditworthiness) and 5(c) (life and health insurance) systems perform an assessment of: the deployer's processes using the system; period and frequency of use; categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected; specific risks of harm to them; human oversight measures; measures to be taken if risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms.

obligations.title: Conformity assessment
obligations.text: High-risk systems undergo conformity assessment before being placed on the market; for most Annex III systems this is internal control (Annex VI).

obligations.title: Registration
obligations.text: Providers (and public-authority deployers) register Annex III high-risk systems in the EU database before placing them on the market or putting them into service.

obligations.title: Post-market monitoring
obligations.text: Providers establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the risk, actively collecting and analysing data on performance throughout the lifetime.

obligations.title: Reporting of serious incidents
obligations.text: Serious incidents are reported to the market surveillance authority immediately after a causal link is established and no later than 15 days after awareness (shorter deadlines for widespread infringements or death).

obligations.title: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
obligations.text: A person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision and the main elements of the decision.

obligations.title: Penalties
obligations.text: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to EUR 15 million or 3% for other obligations; up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities.

team_text: We would like to register an AI use case. The system is called FinScore Retail. The Head of Consumer Finance owns it. It was built in-house by the credit risk analytics team. It is in production since March 2026. It estimates the probability of default of each applicant for personal and auto financing and turns it into a credit score from 300 to 900. Credit officers use the score to approve or decline financing applications from individuals and to set the financing limit; in practice officers follow the score in about 95% of cases. It is used in retail credit and financing decisions. It must not be used for SME or corporate financing, collections or marketing. About 60 credit officers in the central credit unit use it; they completed a two-day training on the score. Individual applicants for personal and auto financing are affected by the decisions. Yes, each score is about one individual applicant. About 12,000 applications a month. Applicants can include elderly customers and people with irregular income; officers can refer them for manual underwriting. No, all applicants are in Pakistan. It recommends; a credit officer makes the decision. A credit officer reviews every application and can override the score with a documented reason; overrides are about 5% of cases. Declined applicants are given the main reasons and can appeal to the credit review desk, where a senior officer re-assesses the file. Application data, salary credits, repayment history, the credit bureau report and existing financing exposures. It processes personal financial data of applicants. No biometric data is used. It was trained on five years of the Bank's own financing applications and repayment outcomes. We checked the training data for gaps by region, gender and age; women and rural applicants were under-represented and we re-weighted them. All data stays in the Bank's onshore data centre in Karachi; only the credit risk team can access it. It is a gradient boosting model. No, it does not generate content; it outputs a score. No, applicants never interact with it; only credit officers see the score. It reads from the loan origination system and the credit bureau, and writes the score back to the loan origination system. On a hold-out set it has a Gini of 0.62 and a KS of 0.45, validated by the model validation team. We compared approval and error rates by gender, age band and province; the largest gap was 3 percentage points, within our 5-point tolerance. Each score comes with the top five reason codes, which officers share with declined applicants. It was tested on missing and extreme values and penetration-tested by IT security before go-live. Model risk reviews the population stability index and default rates monthly, with a full revalidation every year. If performance drops, the Head of Consumer Finance is alerted, the score can be switched off and officers fall back to the manual scorecard. All inputs, scores, overrides and decisions are logged and kept for ten years. The application form tells applicants that an automated credit score is used in the decision. We completed an AI impact assessment covering fundamental rights and data protection; the CRO's office signed it off in February 2026. SBP prudential regulations for consumer financing and consumer protection rules apply, plus Shariah review of the products.

obligations.title: AI literacy
obligations.text: Providers and deployers take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf.

obligations.title: Risk management system
obligations.text: A continuous, iterative risk management process across the lifecycle: identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights; estimate risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluate post-market data; adopt targeted risk management measures; test the system; give specific consideration to persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

obligations.title: Data and data governance
obligations.text: Training, validation and testing data subject to governance practices covering design choices, data collection processes and origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability and suitability, examination for possible biases likely to affect health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases, and identification of data gaps. Data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and as free of errors and complete as possible. Art. 10(5) allows processing special categories of personal data strictly for bias detection and correction, with safeguards.

obligations.title: Technical documentation
obligations.text: Technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date: general description, intended purpose, development process, design specifications, data requirements, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures and metrics, risk management system, changes over the lifecycle, standards applied, post-market monitoring plan.

obligations.title: Record-keeping
obligations.text: Technical capability for automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, enabling identification of risk situations, post-market monitoring and monitoring of operation.

obligations.title: Transparency and information to deployers
obligations.text: Designed so deployers can interpret output and use it appropriately; accompanied by instructions for use with the provider's identity, characteristics, capabilities and limitations, intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances leading to risks, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data specifications, human oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance, and log collection mechanisms.

obligations.title: Human oversight
obligations.text: Designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons during use. Oversight measures enable the assigned persons to: understand capacities and limitations and monitor operation; remain aware of automation bias; correctly interpret output; decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output; intervene or interrupt through a stop button or similar procedure.

obligations.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligations.text: Appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout the lifecycle. Accuracy levels and metrics declared in instructions for use. Resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies; feedback loops addressed; resilient against attempts to alter use or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities (data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks).

obligations.title: Provider obligations and quality management system
obligations.text: Providers ensure compliance with Section 2, have a quality management system, keep documentation and logs, undergo conformity assessment (Art. 43), draw up an EU declaration of conformity (Art. 47), affix CE marking (Art. 48), register (Art. 49), take corrective actions (Art. 20) and demonstrate conformity on request.

obligations.title: Responsibilities along the value chain
obligations.text: A deployer or other third party becomes a provider of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on it, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk.

obligations.title: Deployer obligations
obligations.text: Deployers: use the system according to instructions (26(1)); assign human oversight to persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (26(2)); ensure input data under their control is relevant and sufficiently representative (26(4)); monitor operation and inform the provider, and suspend use if it presents a risk; report serious incidents (26(5)); keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (26(6)); inform workers' representatives before use in the workplace (26(7)); inform natural persons that they are subject to a high-risk system that makes or assists decisions about them (26(11)).

obligations.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
obligations.text: Before deployment, bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III 5(b) (creditworthiness) and 5(c) (life and health insurance) systems perform an assessment of: the deployer's processes using the system; period and frequency of use; categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected; specific risks of harm to them; human oversight measures; measures to be taken if risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms.

obligations.title: Conformity assessment
obligations.text: High-risk systems undergo conformity assessment before being placed on the market; for most Annex III systems this is internal control (Annex VI).

obligations.title: Registration
obligations.text: Providers (and public-authority deployers) register Annex III high-risk systems in the EU database before placing them on the market or putting them into service.

obligations.title: Post-market monitoring
obligations.text: Providers establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the risk, actively collecting and analysing data on performance throughout the lifetime.

obligations.title: Reporting of serious incidents
obligations.text: Serious incidents are reported to the market surveillance authority immediately after a causal link is established and no later than 15 days after awareness (shorter deadlines for widespread infringements or death).

obligations.title: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
obligations.text: A person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision and the main elements of the decision.

obligations.title: Penalties
obligations.text: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to EUR 15 million or 3% for other obligations; up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities.

team_text:
Registration request for a new AI use case. The system is called FinScore Retail. The Head of Consumer Finance owns it. It was built in-house by the credit risk analytics team. It is in production since March 2026. It estimates the probability of default of each applicant for personal and auto financing and turns it into a credit score from 300 to 900. Credit officers use the score to approve or decline financing applications from individuals and to set the financing limit; in practice officers follow the score in about 95% of cases. It is used in retail credit and financing decisions. It must not be used for SME or corporate financing, collections or marketing. About 60 credit officers in the central credit unit use it; they completed a two-day training on the score. Individual applicants for personal and auto financing are affected by the decisions. Yes, each score is about one individual applicant. About 12,000 applications a month. No, all applicants are in Pakistan. A credit officer reviews every application and can override the score with a documented reason; overrides are about 5% of cases. Declined applicants are given the main reasons and can appeal to the credit review desk, where a senior officer re-assesses the file. Application data, salary credits, repayment history, the credit bureau report and existing financing exposures. It processes personal financial data of applicants. It was trained on five years of the Bank's own financing applications and repayment outcomes. We checked the training data for gaps by region, gender and age; women and rural applicants were under-represented and we re-weighted them. All data stays in the Bank's onshore data centre in Karachi; only the credit risk team can access it. It is a gradient boosting model. No, it does not generate content; it outputs a score. No, applicants never interact with it; only credit officers see the score. It reads from the loan origination system and the credit bureau, and writes the score back to the loan origination system. On a hold-out set it has a Gini of 0.62 and a KS of 0.45, validated by the model validation team. We compared approval and error rates by gender, age band and province; the largest gap was 3 percentage points, within our 5-point tolerance. Each score comes with the top five reason codes, which officers share with declined applicants. It was tested on missing and extreme values and penetration-tested by IT security before go-live. Model risk reviews the population stability index and default rates monthly, with a full revalidation every year. If performance drops, the Head of Consumer Finance is alerted, the score can be switched off and officers fall back to the manual scorecard. All inputs, scores, overrides and decisions are logged and kept for ten years. The application form tells applicants that an automated credit score is used in the decision. We completed an AI impact assessment covering fundamental rights and data protection; the CRO's office signed it off in February 2026.

2. No biometric data is used.
3. Applicants can include elderly customers and people with irregular income; officers can refer them for manual underwriting.

obligations.title: AI literacy
obligations.text: Providers and deployers take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf.

obligations.title: Risk management system
obligations.text: A continuous, iterative risk management process across the lifecycle: identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights; estimate risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluate post-market data; adopt targeted risk management measures; test the system; give specific consideration to persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

obligations.title: Data and data governance
obligations.text: Training, validation and testing data subject to governance practices covering design choices, data collection processes and origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability and suitability, examination for possible biases likely to affect health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases, and identification of data gaps. Data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and as free of errors and complete as possible. Art. 10(5) allows processing special categories of personal data strictly for bias detection and correction, with safeguards.

obligations.title: Technical documentation
obligations.text: Technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date: general description, intended purpose, development process, design specifications, data requirements, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures and metrics, risk management system, changes over the lifecycle, standards applied, post-market monitoring plan.

obligations.title: Record-keeping
obligations.text: Technical capability for automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, enabling identification of risk situations, post-market monitoring and monitoring of operation.

obligations.title: Transparency and information to deployers
obligations.text: Designed so deployers can interpret output and use it appropriately; accompanied by instructions for use with the provider's identity, characteristics, capabilities and limitations, intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances leading to risks, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data specifications, human oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance, and log collection mechanisms.

obligations.title: Human oversight
obligations.text: Designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons during use. Oversight measures enable the assigned persons to: understand capacities and limitations and monitor operation; remain aware of automation bias; correctly interpret output; decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output; intervene or interrupt through a stop button or similar procedure.

obligations.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligations.text: Appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout the lifecycle. Accuracy levels and metrics declared in instructions for use. Resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies; feedback loops addressed; resilient against attempts to alter use or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities (data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks).

obligations.title: Provider obligations and quality management system
obligations.text: Providers ensure compliance with Section 2, have a quality management system, keep documentation and logs, undergo conformity assessment (Art. 43), draw up an EU declaration of conformity (Art. 47), affix CE marking (Art. 48), register (Art. 49), take corrective actions (Art. 20) and demonstrate conformity on request.

obligations.title: Responsibilities along the value chain
obligations.text: A deployer or other third party becomes a provider of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on it, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk.

obligations.title: Deployer obligations
obligations.text: Deployers: use the system according to instructions (26(1)); assign human oversight to persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (26(2)); ensure input data under their control is relevant and sufficiently representative (26(4)); monitor operation and inform the provider, and suspend use if it presents a risk; report serious incidents (26(5)); keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (26(6)); inform workers' representatives before use in the workplace (26(7)); inform natural persons that they are subject to a high-risk system that makes or assists decisions about them (26(11)).

obligations.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
obligations.text: Before deployment, bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III 5(b) (creditworthiness) and 5(c) (life and health insurance) systems perform an assessment of: the deployer's processes using the system; period and frequency of use; categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected; specific risks of harm to them; human oversight measures; measures to be taken if risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms.

obligations.title: Conformity assessment
obligations.text: High-risk systems undergo conformity assessment before being placed on the market; for most Annex III systems this is internal control (Annex VI).

obligations.title: Registration
obligations.text: Providers (and public-authority deployers) register Annex III high-risk systems in the EU database before placing them on the market or putting them into service.

obligations.title: Post-market monitoring
obligations.text: Providers establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the risk, actively collecting and analysing data on performance throughout the lifetime.

obligations.title: Reporting of serious incidents
obligations.text: Serious incidents are reported to the market surveillance authority immediately after a causal link is established and no later than 15 days after awareness (shorter deadlines for widespread infringements or death).

obligations.title: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
obligations.text: A person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision and the main elements of the decision.

obligations.title: Penalties
obligations.text: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to EUR 15 million or 3% for other obligations; up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities.

obligations.title: AI literacy
obligations.text: Providers and deployers take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf.

obligations.title: Risk management system
obligations.text: A continuous, iterative risk management process across the lifecycle: identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights; estimate risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluate post-market data; adopt targeted risk management measures; test the system; give specific consideration to persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

obligations.title: Data and data governance
obligations.text: Training, validation and testing data subject to governance practices covering design choices, data collection processes and origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability and suitability, examination for possible biases likely to affect health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases, and identification of data gaps. Data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and as free of errors and complete as possible. Art. 10(5) allows processing special categories of personal data strictly for bias detection and correction, with safeguards.

obligations.title: Technical documentation
obligations.text: Technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date: general description, intended purpose, development process, design specifications, data requirements, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures and metrics, risk management system, changes over the lifecycle, standards applied, post-market monitoring plan.

obligations.title: Record-keeping
obligations.text: Technical capability for automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, enabling identification of risk situations, post-market monitoring and monitoring of operation.

obligations.title: Transparency and information to deployers
obligations.text: Designed so deployers can interpret output and use it appropriately; accompanied by instructions for use with the provider's identity, characteristics, capabilities and limitations, intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances leading to risks, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data specifications, human oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance, and log collection mechanisms.

obligations.title: Human oversight
obligations.text: Designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons during use. Oversight measures enable the assigned persons to: understand capacities and limitations and monitor operation; remain aware of automation bias; correctly interpret output; decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output; intervene or interrupt through a stop button or similar procedure.

obligations.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligations.text: Appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout the lifecycle. Accuracy levels and metrics declared in instructions for use. Resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies; feedback loops addressed; resilient against attempts to alter use or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities (data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks).

obligations.title: Provider obligations and quality management system
obligations.text: Providers ensure compliance with Section 2, have a quality management system, keep documentation and logs, undergo conformity assessment (Art. 43), draw up an EU declaration of conformity (Art. 47), affix CE marking (Art. 48), register (Art. 49), take corrective actions (Art. 20) and demonstrate conformity on request.

obligations.title: Responsibilities along the value chain
obligations.text: A deployer or other third party becomes a provider of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on it, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk.

obligations.title: Deployer obligations
obligations.text: Deployers: use the system according to instructions (26(1)); assign human oversight to persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (26(2)); ensure input data under their control is relevant and sufficiently representative (26(4)); monitor operation and inform the provider, and suspend use if it presents a risk; report serious incidents (26(5)); keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (26(6)); inform workers' representatives before use in the workplace (26(7)); inform natural persons that they are subject to a high-risk system that makes or assists decisions about them (26(11)).

obligations.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
obligations.text: Before deployment, bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III 5(b) (creditworthiness) and 5(c) (life and health insurance) systems perform an assessment of: the deployer's processes using the system; period and frequency of use; categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected; specific risks of harm to them; human oversight measures; measures to be taken if risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms.

obligations.title: Conformity assessment
obligations.text: High-risk systems undergo conformity assessment before being placed on the market; for most Annex III systems this is internal control (Annex VI).

obligations.title: Registration
obligations.text: Providers (and public-authority deployers) register Annex III high-risk systems in the EU database before placing them on the market or putting them into service.

obligations.title: Transparency: interaction with natural persons
obligations.text: Providers ensure AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious from the context.

obligations.title: Post-market monitoring
obligations.text: Providers establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the risk, actively collecting and analysing data on performance throughout the lifetime.

obligations.title: Reporting of serious incidents
obligations.text: Serious incidents are reported to the market surveillance authority immediately after a causal link is established and no later than 15 days after awareness (shorter deadlines for widespread infringements or death).

obligations.title: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
obligations.text: A person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision and the main elements of the decision.

obligations.text: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to EUR 15 million or 3% for other obligations; up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities.

team_text:
Registration request for a new AI use case. It is called QuickCash. The Head of Digital Lending owns it. Built in-house by the digital lending team. It is in production. It decides in seconds whether a customer in the mobile app gets a nano-loan of up to PKR 50,000 and how much. The model approves or declines each nano-loan request and sets the amount, and the money is disbursed immediately. It is a consumer credit use. Not for loans above PKR 50,000. The digital lending team monitors it. Retail customers who request nano-loans in the app. About 90,000 requests a month. Many applicants are low-income and some are financially distressed; there is a cap of three loans a year. No output is used in the EU and no affected people are in the EU. It approves and declines automatically without human review. There is no human review of individual decisions; the team reviews approval rates weekly. Customers can call the helpline to ask about a decline, but there is no formal appeal. App usage, account transactions, salary credits and bureau data. No biometric data. Eighteen months of the Bank's own nano-loan repayment data. We checked missing values but not representativeness. Onshore cloud provider in Pakistan. Logistic regression with a gradient boosting challenger. It does not generate any text, image or other content. Reads from the core banking system and the bureau; writes approvals and disbursement instructions to core banking. AUC of 0.74 on the validation set; default rate is tracked monthly. Decline reasons are generic. Basic input validation and a pen test of the app. Weekly approval and default dashboards reviewed by the lending team. Requests and decisions are logged for five years. obligations.title: AI literacy
obligations.text: Providers and deployers take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf.

obligations.title: Risk management system
obligations.text: A continuous, iterative risk management process across the lifecycle: identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights; estimate risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluate post-market data; adopt targeted risk management measures; test the system; give specific consideration to persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

obligations.title: Data and data governance
obligations.text: Training, validation and testing data subject to governance practices covering design choices, data collection processes and origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability and suitability, examination for possible biases likely to affect health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases, and identification of data gaps. Data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and as free of errors and complete as possible. Art. 10(5) allows processing special categories of personal data strictly for bias detection and correction, with safeguards.

obligations.title: Technical documentation
obligations.text: Technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date: general description, intended purpose, development process, design specifications, data requirements, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures and metrics, risk management system, changes over the lifecycle, standards applied, post-market monitoring plan.

obligations.title: Record-keeping
obligations.text: Technical capability for automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, enabling identification of risk situations, post-market monitoring and monitoring of operation.

obligations.title: Transparency and information to deployers
obligations.text: Designed so deployers can interpret output and use it appropriately; accompanied by instructions for use with the provider's identity, characteristics, capabilities and limitations, intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances leading to risks, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data specifications, human oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance, and log collection mechanisms.

obligations.title: Human oversight
obligations.text: Designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons during use. Oversight measures enable the assigned persons to: understand capacities and limitations and monitor operation; remain aware of automation bias; correctly interpret output; decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output; intervene or interrupt through a stop button or similar procedure.

obligations.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligations.text: Appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout the lifecycle. Accuracy levels and metrics declared in instructions for use. Resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies; feedback loops addressed; resilient against attempts to alter use or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities (data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks).

obligations.title: Provider obligations and quality management system
obligations.text: Providers ensure compliance with Section 2, have a quality management system, keep documentation and logs, undergo conformity assessment (Art. 43), draw up an EU declaration of conformity (Art. 47), affix CE marking (Art. 48), register (Art. 49), take corrective actions (Art. 20) and demonstrate conformity on request.

obligations.title: Responsibilities along the value chain
obligations.text: A deployer or other third party becomes a provider of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on it, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk.

obligations.title: Deployer obligations
obligations.text: Deployers: use the system according to instructions (26(1)); assign human oversight to persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (26(2)); ensure input data under their control is relevant and sufficiently representative (26(4)); monitor operation and inform the provider, and suspend use if it presents a risk; report serious incidents (26(5)); keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (26(6)); inform workers' representatives before use in the workplace (26(7)); inform natural persons that they are subject to a high-risk system that makes or assists decisions about them (26(11)).

obligations.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
obligations.text: Before deployment, bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III 5(b) (creditworthiness) and 5(c) (life and health insurance) systems perform an assessment of: the deployer's processes using the system; period and frequency of use; categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected; specific risks of harm to them; human oversight measures; measures to be taken if risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms.

obligations.title: Conformity assessment
obligations.text: High-risk systems undergo conformity assessment before being placed on the market; for most Annex III systems this is internal control (Annex VI).

obligations.title: Registration
obligations.text: Providers (and public-authority deployers) register Annex III high-risk systems in the EU database before placing them on the market or putting them into service.

obligations.title: Transparency: interaction with natural persons
obligations.text: Providers ensure AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious from the context.

obligations.title: Post-market monitoring
obligations.text: Providers establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the risk, actively collecting and analysing data on performance throughout the lifetime.

obligations.title: Reporting of serious incidents
obligations.text: Serious incidents are reported to the market surveillance authority immediately after a causal link is established and no later than 15 days after awareness (shorter deadlines for widespread infringements or death).

obligations.title: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
obligations.text: A person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision and the main elements of the decision.

obligations.title: Penalties
obligations.text: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to EUR 15 million or 3% for other obligations; up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities.

obligations.title: AI literacy
obligations.text: Providers and deployers take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf.

obligations.title: Risk management system
obligations.text: A continuous, iterative risk management process across the lifecycle: identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights; estimate risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluate post-market data; adopt targeted risk management measures; test the system; give specific consideration to persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

obligations.title: Data and data governance
obligations.text: Training, validation and testing data subject to governance practices covering design choices, data collection processes and origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability and suitability, examination for possible biases likely to affect health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases, and identification of data gaps. Data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and as free of errors and complete as possible. Art. 10(5) allows processing special categories of personal data strictly for bias detection and correction, with safeguards.

obligations.title: Technical documentation
obligations.text: Technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date: general description, intended purpose, development process, design specifications, data requirements, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures and metrics, risk management system, changes over the lifecycle, standards applied, post-market monitoring plan.

obligations.title: Record-keeping
obligations.text: Technical capability for automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, enabling identification of risk situations, post-market monitoring and monitoring of operation.

obligations.title: Transparency and information to deployers
obligations.text: Designed so deployers can interpret output and use it appropriately; accompanied by instructions for use with the provider's identity, characteristics, capabilities and limitations, intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances leading to risks, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data specifications, human oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance, and log collection mechanisms.

obligations.title: Human oversight
obligations.text: Designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons during use. Oversight measures enable the assigned persons to: understand capacities and limitations and monitor operation; remain aware of automation bias; correctly interpret output; decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output; intervene or interrupt through a stop button or similar procedure.

obligations.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligations.text: Appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout the lifecycle. Accuracy levels and metrics declared in instructions for use. Resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies; feedback loops addressed; resilient against attempts to alter use or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities (data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks).

obligations.title: Responsibilities along the value chain
obligations.text: A deployer or other third party becomes a provider of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on it, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk.

obligations.title: Deployer obligations
obligations.text: Deployers: use the system according to instructions (26(1)); assign human oversight to persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (26(2)); ensure input data under their control is relevant and sufficiently representative (26(4)); monitor operation and inform the provider, and suspend use if it presents a risk; report serious incidents (26(5)); keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (26(6)); inform workers' representatives before use in the workplace (26(7)); inform natural persons that they are subject to a high-risk system that makes or assists decisions about them (26(11)).

obligations.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
obligations.text: Before deployment, bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III 5(b) (creditworthiness) and 5(c) (life and health insurance) systems perform an assessment of: the deployer's processes using the system; period and frequency of use; categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected; specific risks of harm to them; human oversight measures; measures to be taken if risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms.

obligations.title: Reporting of serious incidents
obligations.text: Serious incidents are reported to the market surveillance authority immediately after a causal link is established and no later than 15 days after awareness (shorter deadlines for widespread infringements or death).

obligations.title: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
obligations.text: A person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision and the main elements of the decision.

obligations.title: Penalties
obligations.text: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to EUR 15 million or 3% for other obligations; up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities.

team_text:

It is in pilot on 10% of the card portfolio. It re-scores every cardholder's creditworthiness monthly from their spending and repayment behaviour and recommends increasing or decreasing their credit card limit. Limit increases are approved by the cards team, but limit decreases are applied automatically to the cardholder's account. It is a credit limit management use for consumer cards. Not for new card applications. The cards portfolio team. Individual credit cardholders. Yes, each recommendation is about one cardholder. About 45,000 cardholders a month. Elderly cardholders are flagged and excluded from automatic decreases. No output is used in the EU and no affected people are in the EU. Decreases are applied automatically without human review; increases need approval. The cards team approves increases; decreases are reviewed only in a monthly sample. Cardholders can request a limit review through the helpline, which a person handles. Card transactions, repayment history and bureau updates. Personal financial data. It uses no biometric data. The vendor's pooled card data from several banks plus our own history for calibration. The vendor provided a data representativeness report for our portfolio. The vendor processes data in its EU data centre in Ireland. Vendor gradient boosting model. It does not generate any text, image or other content. Nobody interacts with it directly; it runs in the background. Reads from the card management system and writes limit changes to it. The vendor reports a Gini of 0.58 on our back-test. Top three reason codes per decision. The vendor holds ISO 27001 and shared its pen-test summary. Monthly limit-change and delinquency reports reviewed by the cards team. The vendor notifies us within 24 hours and we can disable automatic decreases. All recommendations and changes are logged for seven years. Cardholders are informed by SMS when their limit changes, with the main reason. IT risk and procurement completed due diligence; the contract covers data use, audit rights, incident notice and exit. An impact assessment was completed for the pilot. SBP cloud outsourcing framework applies because data goes offshore; approval was requested.

obligations.title: AI literacy
obligations.text: Providers and deployers take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf.

obligations.title: Risk management system
obligations.text: A continuous, iterative risk management process across the lifecycle: identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights; estimate risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluate post-market data; adopt targeted risk management measures; test the system; give specific consideration to persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

obligations.title: Data and data governance
obligations.text: Training, validation and testing data subject to governance practices covering design choices, data collection processes and origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability and suitability, examination for possible biases likely to affect health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases, and identification of data gaps. Data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and as free of errors and complete as possible. Art. 10(5) allows processing special categories of personal data strictly for bias detection and correction, with safeguards.

obligations.title: Technical documentation
obligations.text: Technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date: general description, intended purpose, development process, design specifications, data requirements, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures and metrics, risk management system, changes over the lifecycle, standards applied, post-market monitoring plan.

obligations.title: Record-keeping
obligations.text: Technical capability for automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, enabling identification of risk situations, post-market monitoring and monitoring of operation.

obligations.title: Transparency and information to deployers
obligations.text: Designed so deployers can interpret output and use it appropriately; accompanied by instructions for use with the provider's identity, characteristics, capabilities and limitations, intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances leading to risks, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data specifications, human oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance, and log collection mechanisms.

obligations.title: Human oversight
obligations.text: Designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons during use. Oversight measures enable the assigned persons to: understand capacities and limitations and monitor operation; remain aware of automation bias; correctly interpret output; decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output; intervene or interrupt through a stop button or similar procedure.

obligations.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligations.text: Appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout the lifecycle. Accuracy levels and metrics declared in instructions for use. Resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies; feedback loops addressed; resilient against attempts to alter use or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities (data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks).

obligations.title: Responsibilities along the value chain
obligations.text: A deployer or other third party becomes a provider of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on it, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk.

obligations.title: Deployer obligations
obligations.text: Deployers: use the system according to instructions (26(1)); assign human oversight to persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (26(2)); ensure input data under their control is relevant and sufficiently representative (26(4)); monitor operation and inform the provider, and suspend use if it presents a risk; report serious incidents (26(5)); keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (26(6)); inform workers' representatives before use in the workplace (26(7)); inform natural persons that they are subject to a high-risk system that makes or assists decisions about them (26(11)).

obligations.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
obligations.text: Before deployment, bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III 5(b) (creditworthiness) and 5(c) (life and health insurance) systems perform an assessment of: the deployer's processes using the system; period and frequency of use; categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected; specific risks of harm to them; human oversight measures; measures to be taken if risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms.

obligations.title: Reporting of serious incidents
obligations.text: Serious incidents are reported to the market surveillance authority immediately after a causal link is established and no later than 15 days after awareness (shorter deadlines for widespread infringements or death).

obligations.title: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
obligations.text: A person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision and the main elements of the decision.

obligations.title: Penalties
obligations.text: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to EUR 15 million or 3% for other obligations; up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities.

team_text:
Registration request for a new AI use case. It is LimitIQ. The Head of Cards owns it. It is a vendor product. It is in pilot on 10% of the card portfolio. It re-scores every cardholder's creditworthiness monthly from their spending and repayment behaviour and recommends increasing or decreasing their credit card limit. Limit increases are approved by the cards team, but limit decreases are applied automatically to the cardholder's account. Not for new card applications. The cards portfolio team. Individual credit cardholders. Yes, each recommendation is about one cardholder. About 45,000 cardholders a month. Elderly cardholders are flagged and excluded from automatic decreases. No output is used in the EU and no affected people are in the EU. Decreases are applied automatically without human review; increases need approval. The cards team approves increases; decreases are reviewed only in a monthly sample. Cardholders can request a limit review through the helpline, which a person handles. Card transactions, repayment history and bureau updates. Personal financial data. The vendor provided a data representativeness report for our portfolio. The vendor processes data in its EU data centre in Ireland. Vendor gradient boosting model. It does not generate any text, image or other content. Nobody interacts with it directly; it runs in the background. Reads from the card management system and writes limit changes to it. The vendor reports a Gini of 0.58 on our back-test. Top three reason codes per decision. The vendor holds ISO 27001 and shared its pen-test summary. Monthly limit-change and delinquency reports reviewed by the cards team. The vendor notifies us within 24 hours and we can disable automatic decreases. All recommendations and changes are logged for seven years. Cardholders are informed by SMS when their limit changes, with the main reason. IT risk and procurement completed due diligence; the contract covers data use, audit rights, incident notice and exit. An impact assessment was completed for the pilot. SBP cloud outsourcing framework applies because data goes offshore; approval was requested.

obligations.title: AI literacy
obligations.text: Providers and deployers take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf.

obligations.title: Risk management system
obligations.text: A continuous, iterative risk management process across the lifecycle: identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights; estimate risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluate post-market data; adopt targeted risk management measures; test the system; give specific consideration to persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

obligations.title: Data and data governance
obligations.text: Training, validation and testing data subject to governance practices covering design choices, data collection processes and origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability and suitability, examination for possible biases likely to affect health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases, and identification of data gaps. Data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and as free of errors and complete as possible. Art. 10(5) allows processing special categories of personal data strictly for bias detection and correction, with safeguards.

obligations.title: Technical documentation
obligations.text: Technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date: general description, intended purpose, development process, design specifications, data requirements, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures and metrics, risk management system, changes over the lifecycle, standards applied, post-market monitoring plan.

obligations.title: Record-keeping
obligations.text: Technical capability for automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, enabling identification of risk situations, post-market monitoring and monitoring of operation.

obligations.title: Transparency and information to deployers
obligations.text: Designed so deployers can interpret output and use it appropriately; accompanied by instructions for use with the provider's identity, characteristics, capabilities and limitations, intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances leading to risks, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data specifications, human oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance, and log collection mechanisms.

obligations.title: Human oversight
obligations.text: Designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons during use. Oversight measures enable the assigned persons to: understand capacities and limitations and monitor operation; remain aware of automation bias; correctly interpret output; decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output; intervene or interrupt through a stop button or similar procedure.

obligations.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligations.text: Appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout the lifecycle. Accuracy levels and metrics declared in instructions for use. Resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies; feedback loops addressed; resilient against attempts to alter use or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities (data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks).

obligations.title: Responsibilities along the value chain
obligations.text: A deployer or other third party becomes a provider of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on it, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk.

obligations.title: Deployer obligations
obligations.text: Deployers: use the system according to instructions (26(1)); assign human oversight to persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (26(2)); ensure input data under their control is relevant and sufficiently representative (26(4)); monitor operation and inform the provider, and suspend use if it presents a risk; report serious incidents (26(5)); keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (26(6)); inform workers' representatives before use in the workplace (26(7)); inform natural persons that they are subject to a high-risk system that makes or assists decisions about them (26(11)).

obligations.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
obligations.text: Before deployment, bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III 5(b) (creditworthiness) and 5(c) (life and health insurance) systems perform an assessment of: the deployer's processes using the system; period and frequency of use; categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected; specific risks of harm to them; human oversight measures; measures to be taken if risks materialise, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms.

obligations.title: Transparency: interaction with natural persons
obligations.text: Providers ensure AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious from the context.

obligations.title: Reporting of serious incidents
obligations.text: Serious incidents are reported to the market surveillance authority immediately after a causal link is established and no later than 15 days after awareness (shorter deadlines for widespread infringements or death).

obligations.title: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
obligations.text: A person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision and the main elements of the decision.

obligations.title: Penalties
obligations.text: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to EUR 15 million or 3% for other obligations; up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities.

team_text:
Registration request for a new AI use case. It is called SplitPay Check. The Head of Partnerships owns it. It is a vendor BNPL decisioning service. The vendor is a BNPL platform provider. It decides at an online merchant's checkout whether a shopper is eligible for buy now, pay later instalments and the instalment limit. It approves or declines the instalment plan in real time. Consumer credit at point of sale. The partnerships team manages it. Shoppers applying for instalments, who may be new to the Bank. Yes, each decision is about an individual shopper. Expected 20,000 checkouts a month. No output is used in the EU and no affected people are in the EU. Fully automated approval and decline. No human reviews individual decisions. Shopper identity data, purchase basket, device data and bureau data. Personal financial data. It uses no biometric data. The vendor's data from other markets. Not done for our market yet. Vendor cloud in Bahrain. Shoppers see the decision at checkout. Reads merchant checkout data and bureau data; writes approved plans to our lending system. The vendor reports 3% default in other markets. No reasons are given to shoppers. Vendor pen-test report received. Monthly default and approval reporting. We can turn off the service at the merchant. Vendor keeps logs for two years. Checkout says the decision is automated. Due diligence is in progress; the contract is being negotiated. SBP BNPL and cloud outsourcing rules apply.

obligations.title: AI literacy
obligations.text: Providers and deployers take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of staff and others operating AI systems on their behalf.

obligations.title: Risk management system
obligations.text: A continuous, iterative risk management process across the lifecycle: identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights; estimate risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluate post-market data; adopt targeted risk management measures; test the system; give specific consideration to persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

obligations.title: Data and data governance
obligations.text: Training, validation and testing data subject to governance practices covering design choices, data collection processes and origin, preparation operations, assumptions, availability and suitability, examination for possible biases likely to affect health, safety or fundamental rights or lead to prohibited discrimination, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate such biases, and identification of data gaps. Data must be relevant, sufficiently representative and as free of errors and complete as possible. Art. 10(5) allows processing special categories of personal data strictly for bias detection and correction, with safeguards.

obligations.title: Technical documentation
obligations.text: Technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date: general description, intended purpose, development process, design specifications, data requirements, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures and metrics, risk management system, changes over the lifecycle, standards applied, post-market monitoring plan.

obligations.title: Record-keeping
obligations.text: Technical capability for automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system, enabling identification of risk situations, post-market monitoring and monitoring of operation.

obligations.title: Transparency and information to deployers
obligations.text: Designed so deployers can interpret output and use it appropriately; accompanied by instructions for use with the provider's identity, characteristics, capabilities and limitations, intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable circumstances leading to risks, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data specifications, human oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance, and log collection mechanisms.

obligations.title: Human oversight
obligations.text: Designed to be effectively overseen by natural persons during use. Oversight measures enable the assigned persons to: understand capacities and limitations and monitor operation; remain aware of automation bias; correctly interpret output; decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output; intervene or interrupt through a stop button or similar procedure.

obligations.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligations.text: Appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout the lifecycle. Accuracy levels and metrics declared in instructions for use. Resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies; feedback loops addressed; resilient against attempts to alter use or performance by exploiting vulnerabilities (data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks).

obligations.title: Responsibilities along the value chain
obligations.text: A deployer or other third party becomes a provider of a high-risk system if it puts its name or trademark on it, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system so that it becomes high-risk.

obligations.title: Deployer obligations
obligations.text: Deployers: use the system according to instructions (26(1)); assign human oversight to persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (26(2)); ensure input data under their control is relevant and sufficiently representative (26(4)); monitor operation and inform the provider, and suspend use if it presents a risk; report serious incidents (26(5)); keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (26(6)); inform workers' representatives before use in the workplace (26(7)); inform natural persons that they are subject to a high-risk system that makes or assists decisions about them (26(11)).

obligations.title: Reporting of serious incidents
obligations.text: Serious incidents are reported to the market surveillance authority immediately after a causal link is established and no later than 15 days after awareness (shorter deadlines for widespread infringements or death).

obligations.title: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
obligations.text: A person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of output from an Annex III high-risk system, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision and the main elements of the decision.

obligations.title: Penalties
obligations.text: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices; up to EUR 15 million or 3% for other obligations; up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities.
